blocks.content: Beyond the basic -p hostPort:containerPort mapping covered in the Docker Containers module, port publishing has real options worth knowing: random port assignment, binding to a specific interface, and protocol selection.
-p 8080:80 forwards traffic from host port 8080 to the container's port 80, the fundamental mechanism that makes a container's service reachable from outside the Docker host at all.

blocks.alt: Host port forwards through to a specific container port

blocks.content: Capital -P publishes every port the image's EXPOSE instructions declare, but lets Docker pick a random, currently-unused host port for each one, instead of you specifying an exact one, useful when running many instances of the same image where fixed ports would collide.

blocks.alt: Docker picks the host port for you, avoiding collisions

blocks.content: 3. Binding to a Specific Host Interface
blocks.text: 3. Binding to a Specific Host Interface

blocks.content: By default a published port listens on every network interface on the host (0.0.0.0). Prefixing the mapping with a specific IP, most commonly 127.0.0.1, restricts it to that interface only, useful for a port that should only be reachable locally, never from the network.

blocks.alt: Restricting a published port to one specific interface

blocks.content:
docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 nginx
# Reachable only from localhost, not from the network at all

code.content:
docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 nginx
# Reachable only from localhost, not from the network at all

codes.bash:
docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 nginx
# Reachable only from localhost, not from the network at all

blocks.content: Port mappings default to TCP, applications using UDP (DNS servers, some game or streaming protocols) need the protocol specified explicitly, and both can even be published on the same port number simultaneously if genuinely needed.

blocks.alt: TCP by default, UDP available with an explicit suffix

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Beyond a fixed -p mapping, -P assigns random host ports automatically, useful for running many instances of the same image without collisions.
A mapping can be restricted to a specific host interface and can specify UDP explicitly when TCP is not the right protocol.
